submissions.findingTextShort: Human pediatric case evidence links oral Margosa/neem seed oil exposure to acute toxic encephalopathy, but the signal is seed-oil and case-report specific.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 2259944 reports toxic encephalopathy after oral Margosa oil, an extract of Neem seed, particularly in infants and young children, with vomiting, drowsiness, tachypnea, recurrent generalized seizures, leukocytosis and metabolic acidosis described. This is clinically important human hazard evidence for acute oral seed-oil exposure, but it must not be generalized to standardized aqueous leaves-and-twigs extract, leaf powder, mouthrinse, bark/root preparations, or ordinary dietary exposure, and a case-report source does not establish incidence or a universal toxic dose.
submissions.populationContext: Infants and young children described in human poisoning cases.
submissions.usageContext: Oral Margosa/neem seed oil exposure; not other Neem plant parts or preparations.
submissions.safetyContext: Supports a preparation-specific pediatric acute-toxicity warning, not a class-wide risk estimate.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Case-report evidence cannot quantify incidence, dose-response, comparative product risk or safety of other Neem preparations. Draft-only pending source governance.

submissions.findingTextShort: Animal neem-oil toxicology identifies testis, liver and kidney as target organs at high experimental exposures, without establishing human organ toxicity.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 23353547 / DOI 10.1016/j.etap.2012.12.015 evaluated acute and 28-day subacute Neem oil toxicity in animals. Histopathology identified testis, liver and kidney as target organs at high experimental exposures, while several routine measures, including serum biochemistry under the stated dose range, did not significantly change. This is a preclinical hazard signal for Neem oil, not evidence that humans using other Neem preparations experience the same organ toxicity, incidence or dose threshold.
submissions.populationContext: Preclinical animal toxicology; no human participants.
submissions.usageContext: Neem oil derived from seeds/fruits under high experimental oral exposure; not standardized aqueous leaf/twig extract or mouthrinse.
submissions.safetyContext: Preserve both target-organ histopathology and negative routine-measure findings; no human transfer.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Species, exposure magnitude, formulation and toxicology-study context prevent direct clinical risk quantification. Draft-only pending governance.

submissions.findingTextShort: In pregnant rats, orally administered Neem seed oil increased fetal malformation/variation frequency, while the tested azadirachtin arm did not show the same signal.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 24184262 / DOI 10.1016/j.jep.2013.10.046 compared pregnant rats receiving Neem seed oil with rats receiving azadirachtin throughout pregnancy. Neem seed oil increased the frequency of fetal malformations/variations, particularly visceral findings, whereas the tested azadirachtin arm did not show a significant fetal-impairment result. The contrast reinforces preparation specificity: this animal study is a reproductive-hazard signal for the tested seed oil regimen and cannot establish human teratogenicity or transfer automatically to isolated azadirachtin, leaf extracts or other Neem products.
submissions.populationContext: Pregnant rats; no human pregnancy data.
submissions.usageContext: Oral Neem seed oil versus azadirachtin throughout rat pregnancy.
submissions.safetyContext: Preparation-specific preclinical reproductive signal; human teratogenicity and incidence remain unestablished.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Animal species, regimen and formulation limit clinical transfer; the null azadirachtin comparison must remain visible. Draft-only pending governance.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 2023 pregnant-rat leaf-extract study found no maternal toxicity, embryotoxicity, fetotoxicity or genotoxicity overall, while retaining a high-dose sternum-ossification finding.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 36963474 / DOI 10.1016/j.jep.2023.116403 tested a spray-dried 30% ethanol Neem leaf extract at 300, 600 or 1200 mg/kg across gestation in Wistar rats. The study reported no maternal toxicity, embryotoxicity, fetotoxicity or genotoxicity overall and no major reproductive-performance or histopathology differences, while supernumerary sternum ossification sites were observed and the highest dose altered sternum ossification. This negative/mixed preclinical result is an essential counterweight to other Neem reproductive-toxicity signals and demonstrates that plant part and preparation matter; it does not establish human pregnancy safety.
submissions.populationContext: Pregnant Wistar rats; no human pregnancy data.
submissions.usageContext: Spray-dried 30% ethanol leaf extract across gestation; distinct from seed oil and purified extracts.
submissions.safetyContext: Preserve negative maternal/fetal/genotoxic findings and the ossification observation together; no human safety inference.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: A reassuring animal result for one leaf extract cannot prove safety in pregnant humans or other Neem formulations. Draft-only pending governance.

submissions.findingTextShort: Purified Neem extracts terminated established pregnancy in rodent and nonhuman-primate experiments, with fertility later returning; this is not human contraceptive evidence.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 9228306 / DOI 10.1111/j.1600-0897.1997.tb00264.x reports pregnancy termination after orally delivered purified Neem extracts in rats and nonhuman primates, with fertility later regained in the studied animals. The experiment is relevant to reproductive-hazard provenance because it includes primate data, but it remains preclinical, uses purified extracts selected for immunomodulatory activity, and cannot be represented as proof of human contraceptive efficacy, a human abortifacient effect, or a clinically transferable dose.
submissions.populationContext: Rats, baboons and monkeys; no human participants.
submissions.usageContext: Purified Neem extracts selected for experimental pregnancy-abrogation activity; not generic Neem supplements.
submissions.safetyContext: Reproductive-hazard signal with explicit nonhuman and preparation boundaries; reversibility observations preserved.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Nonhuman species, experimental purification and purpose-built exposure prevent direct clinical transfer. Draft-only pending source governance.
